learning_goals: Explain what an LLM is and its limits
Describe RAG and its three steps
Show how RAG uses documents to answer a question

analogy.story: A student sits for an open‑book exam. The student can read the textbook before writing the answer.
analogy.mapping: Student = LLM. Textbook = knowledge base. Finding the right page = retrieval. Writing the answer using that page = augment and generate.

worked_example.setting: Riya, a 12th‑grade graduate from Bhopal, wants to know the fee for B.Sc. Computer Science at her college.
worked_example.question: What is the annual fee for B.Sc. Computer Science at Government College Bhopal?
documents: Government College Bhopal prospectus 2024: B.Sc. Computer Science fee ₹12,000 per year.
Government College Bhopal prospectus 2023: B.Sc. Computer Science fee ₹10,000 per year.
worked_example.retrieved: Government College Bhopal prospectus 2024: B.Sc. Computer Science fee ₹12,000 per year.
worked_example.answer_without_rag: The fee is around ₹15,000 per year.
worked_example.answer_with_rag: According to the 2024 prospectus, the fee is ₹12,000 per year.

sections.heading: ## What You Will Learn
sections.goal: Tell the learner the goals of this lesson.
points: You will learn what an LLM is and its limits (K1).
You will learn the full form of RAG and what each word means (K2).
You will learn the three steps: retrieve, augment, generate (K3).
You will learn how documents are prepared for search (K4).
You will learn why RAG helps with fresh and private data (K5).
You will learn one key limitation of RAG (K6).
You will learn that RAG does not change the model (K7).

sections.heading: ## Before We Start: Some Basic Ideas
sections.goal: Explain AI, LLM, training data, knowledge cutoff, and hallucination.
points: A model is a computer program that learns patterns from data (F1).
An LLM is a large language model trained on huge text (F1).
Training data is the text used to teach the model (F1).
Knowledge cutoff is the date after which the model knows nothing (F2).
The model has no private or organisation data it never saw (F3).
Hallucination is when the model makes up wrong but confident answers (F4).

sections.heading: ## What Is RAG?
sections.goal: Define RAG and each word in the name.
points: RAG stands for Retrieval‑Augmented Generation (F5).
Retrieval means finding relevant pieces of information (F5).
Augmented means adding those pieces to the question (F5).
Generation means the LLM writes the answer using the added text (F5).
The idea was first published in a 2020 paper by Patrick Lewis and team (F6).

sections.heading: ## Why Does RAG Matter?
sections.goal: List the main benefits of using RAG.
points: Answers can use up‑to‑date and private information (F11).
Fewer made‑up answers, though not zero (F11).
Answers can show sources so you can check them (F11).
No need to retrain the model; just update the documents (F9, F10).
Cheaper and faster than fine‑tuning the model (F10, F11).

sections.heading: ## How Does RAG Work?
sections.goal: Explain preparation and the three question‑time steps.
points: Preparation: collect documents, split into chunks, turn each chunk into an embedding (a list of numbers that captures meaning) using an embedding model, store in a vector database (F7).
A vector is a list of numbers; a vector database lets you search by meaning (F7).
Semantic search finds chunks whose meaning is closest to the question (F8).
Step 1 Retrieve: turn the question into an embedding, find top‑k similar chunks (F8).
Step 2 Augment: put the retrieved chunks into the prompt with the question and an instruction like "answer using only this information" (F8).
Step 3 Generate: the LLM writes the answer from the question plus the retrieved context (F8).
The model weights stay the same; only the documents change (F9).

sections.heading: ## Example: College Fee Query
sections.goal: Show a concrete Indian example of RAG in action.
points: Riya asks the fee question (worked_example.question).
The system searches the college prospectus stored in the vector database (worked_example.documents).
It retrieves the 2024 fee snippet (worked_example.retrieved).
A plain LLM might guess ₹15,000 (worked_example.answer_without_rag) – a hallucination (F4).
With RAG the answer cites the 2024 prospectus: ₹12,000 (worked_example.answer_with_rag).

sections.heading: ## Key Words to Remember
sections.goal: Recap the technical terms introduced in this lesson.
points: model, LLM, training data, knowledge cutoff, hallucination, prompt, token, retrieval, chunk, embedding, vector, vector database, semantic search, context, augment, generate, fine‑tuning, weights

sections.heading: ## Quick Check
sections.goal: Test understanding with a few questions.
points: What does RAG stand for? – Retrieval‑Augmented Generation.
Which step comes first: retrieve or generate? – Retrieve.
Does RAG change the model weights? – No, the weights stay the same.
What is a chunk? – A small piece of a document used for search.
What is one limitation of RAG? – The answer depends on the quality of retrieved chunks.

sections.heading: ## Summary
sections.goal: Recap the main ideas of the lesson.
points: An LLM learns from training data and has a knowledge cutoff (F1, F2).
It cannot see private data and may hallucinate (F3, F4).
RAG adds a retrieval step before generation so the model uses fresh or private documents (F5, F8).
Documents are split into chunks, turned into embeddings, and stored in a vector database (F7).
At query time the system retrieves, augments the prompt, then generates (F8).
RAG does not retrain the model; updating knowledge means updating documents (F9, F10).
Benefits: up‑to‑date answers, sources, lower cost; limitation: answer quality depends on retrieval (F11, F12).

quiz.q: Which step happens first in RAG: retrieve or generate?
Does RAG change the model weights?
quiz.a: No, the model weights stay the same.
A small piece of a document used for search.
The answer depends on the quality of the retrieved chunks.
